metadata.file_name: Test scores and economic growth  update and extension.pdf
metadata.title: Test scores and economic growth: update and extension

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not estimate student-level models from microdata; instead it uses cross-country test-score summaries from Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) and relates them to per-capita GDP growth from the Maddison Project Database. Because the analysis is conducted at the country level (n=49–50 for the main specifications; n=21 for the TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary specification), there is no student sampling frame and no complex survey weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) to apply. The paper therefore does not require PV handling or replicate-weight procedures typical of PISA/TIMSS microdata analyses. Analysts should treat the test-score inputs as already aggregated country indicators and focus on the regression specification and outlier handling (e.g., excluding Zimbabwe) rather than survey-weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are generated for student-level cognitive achievement scales in ILSA microdata, but this paper uses country-level test-score indicators (average test scores and shares above/below OECD-referenced thresholds) taken from a prior cross-country construction (Hanushek and Woessmann, 2012a). Missing-data handling is not described because the dependent variable is country-level GDP growth and the key education inputs are already aggregated; the only explicit data treatment reported is excluding Zimbabwe as an outlier in the main specification. This omission is best interpreted as a reporting gap for missingness at the country-indicator construction stage, rather than a missing-data problem in an ML/PV estimation pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses the cross-country test-score dataset from Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) for 50 countries (tests in mathematics and science in primary and secondary between 1963 and 2003) and per-capita GDP growth from the Maddison Project Database for 1960–2016. Main specification excludes Zimbabwe as an extreme outlier (reported as a robustness specification including Zimbabwe). For the upper-secondary analysis, uses TIMSS 1995 scores for students in the final year of upper-secondary school, available for 21 countries; no additional country-level inclusion/exclusion rules are reported beyond the availability constraint.

main_findings.dataset_used: Hanushek & Woessmann test scores (primary & secondary; 1963–2003) for 50 countries; linked to Maddison GDP per-capita growth (1960–2016)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 1 (regression): Average test score coefficient 0.013*** (excluding Zimbabwe: 0.014***); Adjusted R2 0.46 (excluding Zimbabwe: 0.80); n=49 (excluding Zimbabwe) and n=50 (including Zimbabwe). Robust standard errors in parentheses.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Hanushek & Woessmann test scores (primary & secondary; 1963–2003) linked to Maddison GDP per-capita growth (1960–2016), the study leveraged Average test score, Years of schooling (1960), and Log GDP per capita (1960) to predict Per-capita GDP growth (1960–2016), finding that a one standard deviation increase in test scores is associated with about a 1.3 percentage-point higher growth rate (and 1.4 when excluding Zimbabwe). This indicates that strengthening education quality—rather than only expanding schooling years—may be a key component of long-term growth strategies, though the paper does not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary (final year) scores for 21 countries; linked to Maddison GDP per-capita growth (1990–2016)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2 (regression): TIMSS 1995 score coefficient 0.006*** (0.002); Years of schooling (1995) coefficient 0.001* (0.0001); (log) GDP per capita coefficient −0.009*** (0.0003); Adjusted R2 0.37; n=21. Robust standard errors in parentheses.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary (final year) scores linked to Maddison GDP per-capita growth (1990–2016), the study leveraged TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary score, Years of schooling (1995), and Log GDP per capita (1960) to predict Per-capita GDP growth (1990–2016), finding that higher upper-secondary test performance is positively associated with later growth (0.61% points higher annual growth per one standard deviation higher TIMSS 1995 score). This indicates that education quality in the upper-secondary stage may matter for economic outcomes, though the analysis remains correlational and does not prove causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: Hanushek & Woessmann test-score distribution indicators (shares above/below OECD-referenced thresholds) for 50 countries; linked to Maddison GDP per-capita growth (1960–2016)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (regression): Share of top-performing students coefficient 0.087*** (excluding Zimbabwe) and 0.106*** (including Zimbabwe); Share reaching basic literacy coefficient 0.018*** (excluding Zimbabwe) and 0.015*** (including Zimbabwe); Adjusted R2 0.79 (excluding Zimbabwe) and 0.64 (including Zimbabwe); n=49 and n=50 respectively. Robust standard errors in parentheses.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Hanushek & Woessmann test-score distribution indicators (shares of top performers and students reaching basic literacy) linked to Maddison GDP per-capita growth (1960–2016), the study leveraged Share of top performers, Share reaching basic literacy, Years of schooling (1960), and Log GDP per capita (1960) to predict Per-capita GDP growth (1960–2016), finding that the share of top-performing students is more strongly associated with growth than the share meeting basic requirements (0.87% vs 0.18% points per 10-percentage-point increase). This indicates that policies targeting both high achievement (enabling gifted students to reach potential) and baseline attainment may be important, while the paper cautions that these estimates do not prove causality.

data.outcome_summary: The paper updates cross-country evidence linking education quality to economic growth by combining country-level test-score indicators from Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) with per-capita GDP growth from the Maddison Project Database. For 1960–2016, it reports that a one standard deviation increase in average test scores is associated with about a 1.3–1.4 percentage-point higher growth rate, with Adjusted R2 rising from 0.46 to 0.80 when test scores are added (Table 1; n=49–50). For upper-secondary quality, TIMSS 1995 scores for 21 countries are associated with later growth (1990–2016), with a coefficient of 0.006*** and Adjusted R2=0.37 (Table 2). Finally, the share of top-performing students shows a much stronger association with growth than the share reaching basic literacy (Table 3; 0.87% vs 0.18% points per 10-percentage-point increase). The study does not establish causality and does not use ML or PV-based student microdata, so survey-weighting and PV handling are not applicable.
